clue.text: Soundly beats opposition. It's child's play !

indicators.note: soundly here means by sound, so the phrase before is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: to beat the opposition is to conquer, giving the word conquers

explanation.surface: A report of someone thrashing rivals, dismissed as mere child's play.
explanation.walkthrough: CONKERS is a British children's game in which horse chestnuts on strings are swung to smash an opponent's; it is said just like 'conquers'.
explanation.definitionFit: The game of horse chestnuts on strings is played by schoolchildren, so it is literally a child's pastime.

clue.text: Fruit could -be the right tonic

indicators.note: could be signals that the letters may be arranged into something else

explanation.surface: A suggestion that a certain fruit might make the ideal mixer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' rearranges R (right) and TONIC; 'the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The citron is a large lemon-like citrus fruit with a thick rind.

clue.text: Funds required to develop Eden almost complete

indicators.note: to develop means to grow into a new form, so these letters are rearranged
almost means not quite, so the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: complete means full

explanation.surface: A fundraising appeal to finish developing the Garden of Eden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to develop' rearranges EDEN to NEED; 'almost' cuts FULL (complete) to FUL.
explanation.definitionFit: 'The needful' is slang for the money needed for something, the cash necessary.

clue.text: With this device climber does better than one gold

parts.note: to excel is to do better, so does better gives excels
one is the Roman numeral I
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A mountaineer with some gadget outperforming a single gold medallist.
explanation.walkthrough: In Longfellow's poem Excelsior, a youth climbs the Alps bearing a banner with this strange device. 'device' is the heraldic sense of a motto or emblem; 'than' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Longfellow's young climber carries a banner whose motto, its device, is the Latin word for higher.

clue.text: Norval's father, distributing free hampers

indicators.note: distributing means spreading out, so the letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A father handing out free hampers, perhaps at Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: In John Home's play Douglas, Norval says 'On the Grampian hills my father feeds his flocks': a shepherd-farmer.
explanation.definitionFit: Norval's father fed his flocks on the Grampian hills, so he kept and raised livestock of wool-bearing animals.

clue.text: Shortage here in France comes in bandy

indicators.note: one piece comes into the middle of another, so the French word goes inside

parts.note: handy means skilful, deft
the French for here is ici

explanation.surface: A complaint that a local shortage is turning up in some bandy place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes in' puts ICI, French for 'here', inside DEFT (handy), giving DEF-ICI-T.
explanation.definitionFit: A deficit is an amount by which something falls short, a lack or insufficiency.

clue.text: Poet so thirsty before study

indicators.note: the poet's name is this word before study, so taking study from the poet's name leaves it

parts.note: John Dryden, the Restoration poet
a den is a study

explanation.surface: A poet so parched before settling down to study.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue says the poet is so: DRYDEN is the answer placed before DEN (study). Take DEN from DRYDEN and the answer remains.
explanation.definitionFit: Dry means thirsty, in need of a drink.

clue.text: Old fellow, of upbringing very Scotch

indicators.note: in a down clue upbringing means bringing up, reading the word from the bottom

parts.note: gey is a Scots word for very

explanation.surface: An elderly man whose upbringing was thoroughly Scottish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upbringing' turns OF upwards to FO; GEY is Scots for 'very', as in 'gey dreich'.
explanation.definitionFit: A fogey is an old-fashioned person, often an elderly man set in his ways.

clue.text: Fancy him in a different race?

indicators.note: him is placed in the middle of the other letters
different signals the letters are put in a different order

explanation.surface: Imagining a man as belonging to another race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'different' rearranges RACE to CERA, and 'in' puts HIM inside it: C-HIM-ERA. 'a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A chimera is a fanciful illusion or wild fantasy, and fancy here is a noun.

clue.text: The: eternal paper-round boy (no lie)

indicators.note: round means around, so the paper is wrapped round the other piece

parts.note: The Times is a newspaper

indicators.note: no lie means the word lie is removed from the name

parts.note: Leslie is a boy's name

explanation.surface: An everlasting paperboy doing his round, and that's the truth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no lie' removes LIE from LESLIE to leave LES, and 'round' puts TIMES round it: TIME-LES-S. 'The' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something eternal lasts for ever and is unaffected by the passage of years.

clue.text: Come to point, in attempt to reveal perfidy

indicators.note: the first pieces are placed in the word for attempt, wrapped by it

parts.note: an attempt is a try
to come to a place is to reach it
E, east, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Someone getting to the point of an attempt, only to uncover betrayal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts REACH plus E inside TRY: T-REACHE-RY. 'to reveal' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Treachery and perfidy are synonyms for betrayal of trust or faithlessness.

clue.text: Fairy-tale lawman

parts.note: the brothers who collected German fairy tales; the elder, Jacob, also gave his name to a law of sound change in Germanic languages

explanation.surface: A sheriff or judge figure out of a fairy story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lawman' suggests a sheriff, but the law here is a linguistic one: Grimm's Law describes consonant shifts in the Germanic languages.
explanation.definitionFit: Jacob Grimm, co-compiler of the famous tales, formulated the phonetic law named after him.

clue.text: Waste of Cornish current?

parts.note: the Fal is a river in Cornwall, and a river is a current

explanation.surface: A question about pollution in a Cornish stream.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fal is a river in Cornwall, south-west England; 'current' stands for the river.
explanation.definitionFit: Offal is the entrails and trimmings of a carcass, originally the parts thrown away as refuse.

clue.text: A slip very unusual with this mark of approval

indicators.note: unusual signals that these letters come in an unexpected new order

explanation.surface: An odd slip of paper bearing an official stamp of approval.
explanation.walkthrough: The Privy Seal was the English monarch's personal seal, applied to documents to authorise them.
explanation.definitionFit: The Privy Seal was a royal seal fixed to documents as authorisation, a formal endorsement.

clue.text: Founders, being less expert with wooden clubs?

definitions.text: Founders, being less expert with wooden clubs?

parts.words: Founders, being less expert with wooden clubs?
parts.note: foundry owners who smelt metal, read as golfers better with the metal-headed clubs than with the woods

explanation.surface: Golfers who are weaker with their woods, or the founders of a business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Founders' are not originators but men who run foundries. In golf, irons are metal clubs and woods are wooden ones, so these masters are better with irons.
explanation.definitionFit: Ironmasters owned or managed ironworks, where metal was founded (cast), so they were founders.

clue.text: Reptiles going two by two, say, for these fruits ?

parts.note: the alligator is a reptile, here in the singular as a modifier

indicators.note: say signals that the next word is heard, not spelt

parts.note: going two by two is going in pairs

explanation.surface: Animals marching two by two, as into the Ark, offered as the name of some fruits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' turns PAIRS (two by two) into PEARS by sound. Alligator pears is an old name for avocados.
explanation.definitionFit: Alligator pears are avocados, named for their rough green skin, and avocados are fruits.

clue.text: Government policy calls for sharing

definitions.meaning: the official line that members of a ruling party are expected to follow
a telephone circuit shared by several subscribers

explanation.walkthrough: A party line is both a political party's official position and an old shared telephone line, where neighbours could listen in.
explanation.definitionFit: A party's agreed policy and a shared telephone circuit both go by this name.

clue.text: Speak thus to inferiors about the landing

definitions.meaning: to guide an aircraft to land by radio instructions

explanation.walkthrough: Air traffic controllers guide a pilot down by radio; one may also speak patronisingly to those seen as beneath one.
explanation.definitionFit: Patronising speech and radio guidance of an aircraft onto the runway share this phrasal verb.

clue.text: Could be an emblem or a trial monument

indicators.note: could be signals that the letters following may be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: A puzzle over whether something is an emblem or a trial run of a monument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Could be' rearranges EMBLEM OR A TRIAL; 'an' is a link. The Albert Memorial is a Victorian monument to Prince Albert in Kensington Gardens, London.
explanation.definitionFit: The Albert Memorial is a large Gothic memorial erected in London for Queen Victoria's consort, a famous landmark.

clue.text: The anti-royalist money business?

definitions.meaning: split, the word reads ..., the cry of someone against monarchy
the trade of lending and keeping money

explanation.walkthrough: Split as BAN KING it is a republican slogan; whole, it is the financial industry.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as two words it is a republican's demand; whole, it is the trade of lenders and deposit-takers.

clue.text: Nudist who followed the earliest precedent

definitions.meaning: a member of an early Christian sect that worshipped naked
a descendant or follower of the first man in Genesis

explanation.walkthrough: The Adamites were sects who went naked in imitation of Adam before the Fall; the first man set the earliest example.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of a nude-worshipping sect, and humans as descendants of the first man of Genesis.

clue.text: The beast used to throw stones

definitions.meaning: an ancient catapult or siege engine

explanation.walkthrough: The onager is an Asian wild ass, and also a Roman torsion catapult named for the ass's kick.
explanation.definitionFit: Both an Asian wild ass and a Roman catapult that hurled rocks bear this name.

clue.text: The Fabulous stork one of these flycatchers?

definitions.text: The Fabulous stork one of these flycatchers?

parts.words: The Fabulous stork one of these flycatchers?
parts.note: in Aesop's fable the frogs ask for a ruler and are sent a stork, a bird made monarch; the American flycatchers bear that title in their name

explanation.surface: A question whether the stork of legend belongs to a family of flycatching birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fabulous' means from a fable: in Aesop's The Frogs Who Desired a King, Jupiter sends a stork to rule them, and it eats them. Kingbirds are American tyrant flycatchers.
explanation.definitionFit: Kingbirds are a genus of tyrant flycatchers, and the fable's stork was literally a bird made sovereign.

clue.text: Note for the lineswoman ?

annotationWithheld.why: Note for the lineswoman ? (5): the grid gives B?E?E, BREVE, but no reading of 'for the lineswoman' as a definition or wordplay for BREVE could be confirmed

clue.text: Long tale about the East

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for tale is wrapped round the letter

parts.note: a tale is a yarn
E is the abbreviation for East

explanation.surface: A lengthy story about the Orient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts E inside YARN, giving Y-E-ARN. 'Long' is a verb, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: To long for something is to pine or crave it.

clue.text: Arch Fund appeal?

definitions.meaning: read as two words: oh, give!

explanation.walkthrough: An ogive is a pointed arch in Gothic architecture; split as 'O give' it is a cry for donations.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogive is the architect's term for a pointed arch, and split up it is a plea for donations.

clue.text: Like a chairman showing partiality in advance

parts.note: pre is the prefix meaning before or in advance
siding with someone is showing partiality towards them

explanation.surface: A chairman accused of taking sides before a meeting even starts.
explanation.definitionFit: A chairman presides over a meeting, so one who is chairing it is in the act of presiding.

clue.text: Hell of a card-game!

definitions.meaning: the bottomless ..., the abyss of the damned
a fast trading card game imitating a commodities exchange

explanation.walkthrough: Pit is a card game simulating trading on a commodity exchange; 'the pit' is a biblical name for hell. 'of a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The abyss of the damned and a noisy card game of trading both have this name.

clue.text: Perhaps electing to dismiss one for careless omission

indicators.note: perhaps signals the letters of the word are rearranged, after something is dismissed from them

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Someone electing to sack a player because of a careless omission.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' rearranges ELECTING and 'to dismiss one' removes I from the pool: the remaining letters make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Neglect is failure to attend to something, a careless leaving undone.

clue.text: Kipling's more deadly female

parts.note: Kipling's poem The Female of the Species opens with the female grizzly that rends the peasant, more deadly than the male

explanation.surface: A literary reference to Kipling's claim that the female is deadlier.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's poem The Female of the Species begins with a female bear that, when accosted, 'rends the peasant tooth and nail', and concludes that the female is more deadly than the male.
explanation.definitionFit: The female bear in Kipling's poem is his first example of the female being deadlier than the male.
